To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

students in the MBA programs studied in this investigation ranked face‐to‐ face, teacher‐directed instructional delivery highly but also recognized the benefits of an independent, online instructional environment.

students from Confucius‐heritage countries studying in a trans‐national MBA program in English and Chinese preferred teacher‐directed instruction, and that they preferred face‐to‐ face delivery of instruction, but they also recognised that independent, online instruction had advantages.

students from Confucius‐heritage backgrounds who were studying a transnational MBA program, in which they studied both online and face‐to‐ face, ranked teacher‐direct instruction in the face‐ to‐ face environment as their preferred instructional approach.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question: how does a transnational, intensive, mixed mode MBA program best assist students to achieve their learning goals?
how students learn in the context of an international MBA program, and the implications this has for lecturers.
the instructional preferences of transnational MBA students and how these may be accommodated in the design and delivery of teaching and learning arrangements.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the students in this transnational MBA program have a strong preference for face‐to‐ face instruction and teacher‐centred learning, but that they are also willing to learn in an independent online environment.
the findings of this study provide a valuable starting point to understanding students’ instructional preferences.

this study has provided some preliminary insights into the instructional preferences and learning behaviours of MBA students in Confucian‐ heritage countries and has provided lecturers with some insights into how they can best assist students to meet the objectives of the MBA.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we are able to demonstrate that the students’ instructional communication needs are not being met by the teaching and learning arrangements of the transnational MBA program and that there is a need for a review of these arrangements.
the findings of this study have implications for both teaching and learning.
we are able to provide some insights into the instructional communication preferences of MBA students from Confucius‐heritage backgrounds.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the students’ instructional communication preference is a complex phenomenon that is influenced by a range of factors including the students’ learning style, their cultural backgrounds, the teaching and learning environment, the learning task and the learning context.
it is essential for lecturers to have a good understanding of the students as learners, their instructional preferences and their learning styles.
lecturers need to be mindful of the instructional preferences of transnational students when planning their teaching and learning arrangements.
